sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Craniospinal Irradiation (CSI) with Proton Beam Therapy
sectionToMerge.intro: These answers explain how craniospinal irradiation using proton beam therapy works, who it may suit, and what international patients and caregivers commonly ask before treatment.

groups.title: Understanding Craniospinal Irradiation with Proton Therapy

items.q: What is craniospinal irradiation (CSI) with proton beam therapy?
items.a: Craniospinal irradiation with proton beam therapy is a radiation treatment that targets the entire brain and spinal cord using protons instead of conventional X-rays. It is used mainly for cancers that can spread through the cerebrospinal fluid, such as medulloblastoma. Protons deposit most of their energy directly in the target and stop, which may reduce radiation reaching the heart, lungs, and other healthy tissues. Treatment planning is decided by the radiation oncology team.

items.q: How does proton CSI differ from conventional photon radiation?
items.a: Proton CSI differs from photon (X-ray) CSI mainly in how radiation is delivered beyond the target. Photons continue passing through the body and expose tissues in front of and behind the spine, while protons stop at a set depth, so little to no exit dose reaches organs like the heart, lungs, thyroid, and bowel. This may lower certain long-term risks, though outcomes depend on the individual case and specialist assessment.

items.q: Which cancers are treated with craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: Craniospinal proton therapy is most often used for tumours that can spread along the brain and spinal cord through cerebrospinal fluid. These include medulloblastoma, some ependymomas, germ cell tumours, and certain cases of leukaemia or lymphoma involving the central nervous system. It may be considered for selected children and adults depending on tumour type, stage, and risk. The treating oncology team confirms whether CSI is appropriate after full evaluation.

Craniospinal irradiation works by delivering radiation to the whole brain and spinal cord to destroy cancer cells and any microscopic disease spreading through the cerebrospinal fluid. With proton therapy, beams are shaped to match the target volume so that surrounding healthy organs receive less radiation. This is usually followed by an additional focused radiation boost to the main tumour site. The full plan depends on diagnosis, age, and specialist review.

items.q: Who is eligible for craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: Eligibility for craniospinal proton therapy depends on cancer type, stage, tumour spread, age, and overall health. It may be suitable for selected patients with central nervous system tumours that require whole brain and spine treatment, and it is often considered for children to reduce radiation to developing organs. Final eligibility is decided by the radiation oncology team after reviewing imaging, pathology, and clinical condition, alongside proton centre capacity and availability.

items.q: Is proton CSI suitable for all cancer patients?
items.a: Proton CSI is not suitable for all cancer patients and is used only for specific tumours that require whole brain and spinal cord treatment. Suitability depends on diagnosis, disease spread, prior treatment, age, and overall fitness for radiation. Some patients may be better treated with conventional radiation or other approaches. Whether proton CSI is appropriate should be discussed with a qualified oncology team, and final decisions rest with the treating specialists.

items.q: What happens during craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: During craniospinal proton therapy, the patient lies still on a treatment couch while proton beams are directed at the brain and spine according to a detailed plan. Sessions are painless and usually take several minutes, given daily over multiple weeks. A custom mould or mask helps keep the body in the same position each time. Young children may need sedation or anaesthesia. The exact schedule is set by the treating team.

items.q: What are the side effects of craniospinal proton irradiation?
items.a: Side effects of craniospinal proton irradiation can include fatigue, hair loss, skin changes, nausea, and lowered blood counts, and some effects may appear months or years later. Because protons reduce radiation to organs beyond the target, certain long-term risks may be lower than with conventional radiation, though this varies by patient. Effects depend on age, dose, and treatment area. Side effects should be monitored and managed by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Why is proton CSI often considered for children?
items.a: Proton CSI is often considered for children because their bodies are still developing and more sensitive to radiation. By stopping at the target and delivering little exit dose, proton therapy may reduce radiation to the heart, lungs, thyroid, bowel, and growth centres, which could lower some long-term and growth-related risks. This potential benefit is weighed against tumour type and other factors. The paediatric oncology team makes the final treatment decision.

items.q: How much does craniospinal proton therapy cost?
items.a: The cost of craniospinal proton therapy varies widely and cannot be fixed in advance, as it depends on the country, hospital, number of sessions, need for anaesthesia, imaging, and any supportive care. Proton therapy is generally more expensive than conventional radiation because of the specialised equipment involved. Final cost also depends on diagnosis, stage, complications, and length of stay. A personalised estimate should be obtained from the treating hospital after review.

items.q: Is proton craniospinal irradiation available in India?
items.a: Proton craniospinal irradiation is available at select proton therapy centres in India, though the number of facilities remains limited compared with conventional radiation. Availability depends on the centre's capacity, the patient's diagnosis, and scheduling. Some international patients travel to India for proton therapy, while others seek it elsewhere. Whether treatment can proceed depends on hospital acceptance and medical review, and options should be confirmed directly with the chosen proton centre.

items.q: Which countries offer craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: Craniospinal proton therapy is offered in several countries with proton centres, including the United States, Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, China, India, and others. Because proton facilities require major infrastructure, they are not available everywhere, and capacity can be limited. Where a patient can be treated depends on availability, cost, travel feasibility, and hospital acceptance after medical review. The choice of country should be discussed with the oncology team and treatment coordinators.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: There are clinical trials studying craniospinal proton therapy, often focusing on reducing side effects, refining radiation dose, or improving outcomes in tumours like medulloblastoma. Enrollment is not guaranteed, as trials have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria and eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment. Participation may or may not provide benefit. Patients interested in trials should discuss suitable options with their oncology team and the trial centre.

items.q: What is the difference between pencil beam scanning and passive scattering for CSI?
items.a: Pencil beam scanning and passive scattering are two ways of delivering proton CSI. Passive scattering spreads the proton beam to cover the target using physical devices, while pencil beam scanning steers a narrow beam point by point to shape the dose more precisely. Pencil beam scanning may allow better sparing of healthy tissue in complex spine treatments, though the best technique depends on the case and the equipment available at the treating centre.

items.q: Can proton CSI be combined with chemotherapy?
items.a: Proton CSI is often combined with chemotherapy for many central nervous system tumours, such as medulloblastoma, as part of a multi-step treatment plan. Chemotherapy may be given before, during, or after radiation depending on the diagnosis, risk group, and age. Combining treatments aims to improve disease control, but timing and drug choice vary for each patient. The overall plan and sequencing are decided by the treating oncology and radiation team.

items.q: How can international patients access craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: International patients can access craniospinal proton therapy by sending medical records to a proton centre for review and requesting a treatment plan and cost estimate. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Planning usually includes a second opinion, travel arrangements, and follow-up care. Coordination with the treating centre helps confirm whether treatment can realistically proceed.

items.q: What medical reports are needed for a proton CSI evaluation?
items.a: A proton CSI evaluation usually requires recent MRI scans of the brain and full spine, the pathology or biopsy report, surgical notes, and details of any prior treatment such as surgery or chemotherapy. Blood tests, staging information, and a summary from the treating doctor are also helpful. Complete, up-to-date reports allow the radiation oncology team to assess suitability accurately. Additional tests may be requested after the initial review of records.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with craniospinal proton therapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant proton therapy centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support for craniospinal proton therapy. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, tumour type, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax does not replace doctors or hospitals and cannot guarantee acceptance, cost, or treatment outcomes for any patient.
